subject: English
title: Comprehension and Summary
outline: Figures of speech and figurative language

modules.title: Figures of speech in passages
modules.html:
Writers use figurative language to make ideas vivid. Common figures include:

  • Simile — comparison with as / like: brave as a lion.
  • Metaphor — direct comparison: Time is a thief.
  • Personification — giving human qualities to things: the sun smiled.
  • Hyperbole — exaggeration for effect: I've told you a million times.
  • Litotes — understatement: not bad (= very good).
  • Oxymoron — apparent contradiction: deafening silence.
  • Alliteration — repeated initial sounds: slippery snakes.
  • Onomatopoeia — words that imitate sounds: buzz, clang, hiss.
  • Irony — meaning opposite of the literal: a fire station burnt down (situational).
  • Euphemism — mild expression: passed away (= died).

examples.q: Identify the figure: The waves danced along the shore.
examples.a: Personification — waves given the human action of dancing.

modules.title: Drawing inferences
modules.html:
An inference is a reasonable conclusion drawn from what a passage says, not stated directly.

Ask: What does the writer expect me to understand without saying it aloud?

Steps:

  1. Note the exact words and details in the passage.
  2. Combine those details with common knowledge.
  3. Choose the option that fits the passage evidence — not just your feelings.

Beware of over-inferring: any conclusion must be justified by something the writer wrote.

Key points

  • Direct comparison.
  • Uses like.

Worked example

Q: Time is a thief is an example of:
A: metaphor

Q: She sings like an angel is an example of:
A: simile

examples.q: From Ada glanced at her watch and quickened her pace, what can you infer?
examples.a: That Ada was afraid of being late.

modules.title: Summary of an argumentative passage
modules.html:
An argumentative passage puts forward a case with reasons. Its summary must list those reasons, not merely restate the topic.

Bullet-point method

  1. State the writer's main claim in one sentence.
  2. List each reason or piece of evidence as one bullet — in your own words.
  3. Answer only the number of points asked (say, four reasons).
  4. Keep to the word limit.

Key points

  • Persuasion by reason.
  • Paraphrase in your own words.

Worked example

Q: An argumentative passage aims to:
A: persuade with reasons

Q: In summary, quoting long passages is:
A: not allowed / avoid

More key points

  • An argumentative passage aims to: — persuade with reasons.
  • In summary, quoting long passages is: — not allowed / avoid.
  • A good summary bullet is: — one clear sentence per point.
  • How many points should you give in summary — exactly the number asked.

examples.q: If asked for four reasons the writer opposes plastic bags, what should you list?
examples.a: Four separate, non-overlapping reasons, each rephrased in your own words and drawn only from the passage.

modules.title: Making inferences from texts
modules.html:
Making inferences from texts is a key part of Comprehension and Summary (SSS 2, English). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • Learn the meaning of making inferences from texts and the terms used with it.
  • Know the main types, features or steps involved in making inferences from texts.
  • Be able to give an example of making inferences from texts and explain why it matters in comprehension and summary.
  • Practise past questions on making inferences from texts until you can answer them without notes.

Worked example

Q: Time is a thief is an example of:
A: metaphor — Direct comparison.

Q: She sings like an angel is an example of:
A: simile — Uses like.

She sings like an angel is an example of:
